'''Bartel Leendert van der Waerden''' ({{IPA|nl|ˈbɑrtə(l) ˈleːndərt fɑn dər ˈʋaːrdə(n)|lang}}; 2 February 1903&nbsp;– 12 January 1996) was a [[Dutch people|Dutch]] [[mathematician]] and [[History of mathematics|historian of mathematics]].

==Biography==

===Education and early career===
Van der Waerden learned advanced mathematics at the [[University of Amsterdam]] and the [[University of Göttingen]], from 1919 until 1926. He was much influenced by [[Emmy Noether]] at [[Göttingen]], [[Germany]]. Amsterdam awarded him a Ph.D. for a thesis on [[algebraic geometry]], supervised by Hendrick de Vries.<ref name=math>{{MathGenealogy|id=30607}}</ref> Göttingen awarded him the [[habilitation]] in 1928. In that year, at the age of 25, he accepted a professorship at the [[University of Groningen]].

At 27, Van der Waerden published his ''[[Moderne Algebra]]'', an influential two-volume treatise on [[abstract algebra]], still cited, and perhaps the first treatise to treat the subject as a comprehensive whole. This work systematized an ample body of research by [[Emmy Noether]], [[David Hilbert]], [[Richard Dedekind]], and [[Emil Artin]]. In the following year, 1931, he was appointed professor at the [[University of Leipzig]].

In July 1929, he married Camilla Juliana Anna Rellich, the sister of mathematician [[Franz Rellich]].  They had three children.

===Nazi Germany===
After the [[Nazi Germany|Nazis]] [[Machtergreifung|seized power]], and through [[World War II]], Van der Waerden remained at Leipzig, and passed up opportunities to leave Nazi Germany for [[Princeton University|Princeton]] and [[Utrecht University|Utrecht]]. However, he was critical of the Nazis and refused to give up his Dutch nationality, both of which led to difficulties for him.<ref>Soifer, pp. 393–417.</ref>

===Postwar career===
Following the war, Van der Waerden was repatriated to the Netherlands rather than returning to [[Leipzig]] (then under Soviet control), but struggled to find a position in the Dutch academic system, in part because his time in Germany made his politics suspect and in part due to [[Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer|Brouwer]]'s opposition to Hilbert's school of mathematics. After a year visiting [[Johns Hopkins University]] and two years as a part-time professor, in 1950, Van der Waerden filled the chair in mathematics at the University of Amsterdam.<ref>Soifer, pp. 418–474.</ref> In 1951, he moved to the [[University of Zurich]], where he spent the rest of his career, supervising more than 40 [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D. students]]. 

In 1949, Van der Waerden became member of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]], in 1951 this was changed to a foreign membership.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dwc.knaw.nl/biografie/pmknaw/?pagetype=authorDetail&aId=PE00003703 |title=Bartel Leendert van der Waerden (1903–1996) |publisher=Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences |access-date=8 June 2020}}</ref> In 1973 he received the ''[[Pour le Mérite]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.orden-pourlemerite.de/mitglieder/bartel-leendert-van-der-waerden |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200608194839/http://www.orden-pourlemerite.de/mitglieder/bartel-leendert-van-der-waerden |title=Bartel Leendert van der Waerden |language=de |publisher=Orden Pour le Mérite |archive-date=8 June 2020}}</ref>

==Contributions==
Van der Waerden is mainly remembered for his work on [[abstract algebra]]. He also wrote on [[algebraic geometry]], [[topology]], [[number theory]], [[geometry]], [[combinatorics]], [[mathematical analysis|analysis]], [[probability]] and [[statistics]], and [[quantum mechanics]] (he and [[Heisenberg]] had been colleagues at Leipzig). In later years, he turned to the [[history of mathematics]] and [[History of science|science]]. His historical writings include ''Ontwakende wetenschap'' (1950), which was translated into English as ''Science Awakening'' (1954),<ref>{{cite journal|author=Sarton, George|author-link=George Sarton|journal=Isis|volume=46|number=4|pages=368–369|title=Review of ''Science Awakening'' by B. L. Van der Waerden, translated by Arnold Dresden|date=December 1955|doi=10.1086/348434}}</ref> ''Sources of Quantum Mechanics'' (1967),<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.3035086|title=Review of ''Sources of Quantum Mechanics'' edited with a 59-page historical introduction by B. L. van der Waerden|year=1968|author=Weber, Robert L.|journal=Physics Today|volume=21|issue=7|page=97}}</ref> ''Geometry and Algebra in Ancient Civilizations'' (1983), and ''A History of Algebra'' (1985).<ref>{{cite journal | last=Winter | first=David J. | title=A History of Algebra . By B. L. van der Waerden | journal=The American Mathematical Monthly | volume=95 | issue=8 | date=1988 | doi=10.1080/00029890.1988.11972088 | pages=781–785}}</ref>

Van der Waerden has over 1000 [[academic genealogy|academic descendants]], most of them through three of his students, [[David van Dantzig]] (Ph.D. Groningen 1931), [[Herbert Seifert]] (Ph.D. Leipzig 1932), and Hans Richter (Ph.D. Leipzig 1936, co-advised by [[Paul Koebe]]).<ref name=math/>
